findings.claim: Mary, Queen of Scots described as 'a granddaughter of Henry VII through a legitimate Tudor line'.
findings.truth: She was Henry VII's GREAT-granddaughter: Henry VII > Margaret Tudor > James V > Mary. Lesson 4's own mark scheme says great-granddaughter, so the lessons contradict each other.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Mary, Queen of Scots' and 'Margaret Tudor' descent; lesson 4 practice_questions[0].marks

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: 'Mary, Queen of Scots, granddaughter of Henry VII through a legitimate Tudor line.'
findings.truth: Great-granddaughter. The same error as F1, in the card a student memorises.
findings.evidence: as F1

findings.claim: 'Elizabeth needed a settlement that would not trigger civil war — the lesson of France in the 1560s loomed large.'
findings.truth: Anachronism. The settlement was drafted in 1558-59; the French Wars of Religion began in 1562. Replaced with the German religious wars, which the Peace of Augsburg ended in 1555.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'French Wars of Religion' (1562-98); 'Peace of Augsburg' (1555)

findings.claim: Every lesson sets two practice questions typed '8 marks — Explain Why' (22 across the unit).
findings.truth: Paper 2's British depth study is 32 marks and uses three forms only: describe two features (4), explain why (12) and a choice of judgement question (16). No 8-mark 'explain why' exists on this paper; the period-study 8-markers are consequence, narrative account and importance, which are different forms. All 22 are converted to the real 12-mark form — two stimulus bullets taken from each question's own indicative content plus 'You must also use information of your own' — and the band ladder raised from two reasons to three. This finding covers lessons 1 to 11.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section: Paper 2 booklet B, 32 marks, describing features / causation / judgement

findings.claim: 'Only around 250 to 400 of these clergy refused, alongside 27 of England's 30 surviving Marian bishops.'
findings.truth: There were not 30 sitting Marian bishops. About 20 bishops sat in the Lords and seven, including Cardinal Pole, had died in 1558. Almost every surviving Marian bishop refused the oath; only Anthony Kitchin of Llandaff conformed and kept his see.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Elizabethan Religious Settlement' (twenty bishops; seven died in 1558; all but two lost their posts, Kitchin of Llandaff and the absentee Stanley of Sodor and Man)

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Roughly how many of England's 30 surviving Marian bishops refused the oath of supremacy?' / '27 of the 30 surviving Marian bishops.'
findings.truth: Both the question and the answer rest on the invented figure. The card is rewritten around the fact that almost all refused and only Llandaff conformed.
findings.evidence: as F5

findings.claim: 'examiners reward answers that explain the settlement as a deliberate compromise' and 'Examiners' reports flag candidates who confuse the 1559 settlement with later anti-Catholic legislation'.
findings.truth: An unevidenced assertion about examiner behaviour and an invented examiners'-report provenance. Both rewritten as direct advice; the factual content (12d in 1559, not the 1581 fines) is correct and kept.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: Mark scheme: 'the political need to avoid civil war over religion as had happened in France'.
findings.truth: In 1559 it had not happened in France. The same anachronism as F3.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'French Wars of Religion' (from 1562)

findings.claim: 'For 16-mark questions about the threat to the religious settlement, examiners want analysis — not lists.'
findings.truth: Invented exam claim. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: 'It was backed by the Pope, Mary, Queen of Scots, and foreign powers like Spain.'
findings.truth: A comma-separated list of three items, which the flashcard validator rejects. Rewritten as one idea.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: Key fact: 'Mary was Elizabeth's first cousin once removed, granddaughter of Henry VII through his eldest daughter Margaret Tudor.'
findings.truth: Great-granddaughter. 'First cousin once removed' is correct and is kept.
findings.evidence: as F1

findings.claim: 'Henry VII of England had two daughters who survived to adulthood: Mary Tudor (Elizabeth's grandmother by no line, since Elizabeth descended from Henry VII through his son Henry VIII) and Margaret Tudor, who married James IV of Scotland.'
findings.truth: Incoherent and wrong. Mary Tudor was not Elizabeth's grandmother in any sense; she was Elizabeth's aunt. Margaret (born 1489) was the elder and Mary (born 1496) the younger, and the lesson elsewhere calls Margaret 'his eldest daughter'. Rewritten so the elder daughter comes first and Elizabeth's own descent is stated separately.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Henry VII of England' children; 'Mary Tudor, Queen of France'

findings.claim: 'The Scottish Parliament, led by John Knox, had abolished the authority of the Pope and made Catholic Mass illegal.'
findings.truth: Knox sat in no parliament and led none. He was the leading preacher of the Scottish Reformation and drafted the Scots Confession that the Reformation Parliament of August 1560 adopted. Changed to 'urged on by the preacher John Knox'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Scottish Reformation Parliament' (August 1560)

findings.claim: 'examiners' reports note that strong students show the chain of consequences'.
findings.truth: Invented examiners'-report claim. Trimmed to the advice itself.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: 'the 2023 examiner report flagged vague references to "the Council" as the difference between the top and middle bands', plus 'examiners want you to explain at least three reasons'.
findings.truth: A fabricated citation of a named report. Deleted; the advice to name Cecil, Sussex or Walsingham is kept.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: 'The 2023 Edexcel examiners' report flagged candidates who treated the Privy Council as a vague entity.'
findings.truth: The same fabricated 2023 report, this time in the lesson body. Replaced with direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward answers that connect the plots into a chain rather than describing each in turn.'
findings.truth: Invented exam claim. Rewritten as an instruction.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: 'Ridolfi (1571) produced the 1571 Treasons Act and tightened recusancy fines.'
findings.truth: Sequence error. The Treason Act 1571 had royal assent on 29 May 1571; Ridolfi's plot was not exposed until Norfolk's arrest warrant on 7 September 1571. Lesson 5 attributes the Act to the Northern Rebellion and the 1570 bull, so the two lessons contradict each other. Replaced with Norfolk's execution and the parliamentary pressure on Mary.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Ridolfi plot' (Baillie arrested 12 April 1571; Norfolk arrest warrant 7 September 1571; executed 2 June 1572); lesson 5 content_html

findings.claim: Knowledge check stem: Phelippes 'forged a postscript asking Mary to name her fellow plotters'.
findings.truth: Reversed. Phelippes added the postscript to Mary's reply and it asked BABINGTON to name his fellow conspirators. The lesson body states this correctly, so the knowledge check teaches the opposite of the article.
findings.evidence: lesson 6 content_html; Wikipedia, 'Babington Plot'

findings.claim: The 4-mark mark scheme repeats the same reversal: 'added a forged postscript asking Mary to name fellow plotters'.
findings.truth: As F19. A second mark scheme in the same lesson gets it right ('asking Babington to name his fellow plotters').
findings.evidence: as F19

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: 'To assassinate Elizabeth, free Mary, and welcome a Spanish-backed invasion.'
findings.truth: A comma-separated list of three items, which the flashcard validator rejects. Rewritten as one idea.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: 'Dutch Protestant rebels began the Eighty Years' War in 1568, and Philip's response was to send his most ruthless commander, the Duke of Alva, with 10,000 men.'
findings.truth: Effect given as cause. Alva reached the Netherlands in August 1567, sent in response to the unrest of 1566; the war conventionally dates from 1568, after he arrived. Rewritten as 1566 unrest, then Alva in 1567, then open war from 1568.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Fernando Alvarez de Toledo, 3rd Duke of Alba' (arrived 1567); 'Eighty Years' War'

findings.claim: 'By the mid-1580s a single major incident — English involvement in the Netherlands and Drake's raid on Cadiz — had made war unavoidable.'
findings.truth: Internally contradictory ('a single major incident', then two are named) and misdated: the Cadiz raid was April 1587, not the mid-1580s. Rewritten as 'By 1587 two decisive moves'.
findings.evidence: lesson 7's own dates (Nonsuch August 1585; Cadiz 19 April 1587)

findings.claim: 'examiners want at least three reasons explained AND interconnected'.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim. Rewritten as an instruction.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: The 16-mark question carries 'SPaG marks are awarded for accurate spelling, punctuation and use of period-specific historical terminology', and its mark scheme awards SPaG in every band.
findings.truth: Paper 2 carries no SPaG marks at all. The spec gives the qualification 8 SPaG marks and puts every one of them on Paper 1 Question 5/6 (4 marks) and Paper 3 Question 3(d) (4 marks). A student rationing time for SPaG on this paper is chasing marks that do not exist. All SPaG wording removed from the question and the mark scheme.
findings.evidence: spec: 'The total qualification mark is 168, of which 8 marks are for spelling, punctuation, grammar...'; the Paper 1 and Paper 3 assessment sections name the only SPaG questions

findings.claim: Opening paragraph: 'Examiners reward students who can explain why'.
findings.truth: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour. Rewritten as 'A strong answer explains why'.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: 'Edexcel examiners specifically flag "the weather beat the Armada" as a single-factor answer that caps below the top band.'
findings.truth: A fabricated claim about a board's marking behaviour. The underlying point (a judgement question needs several factors weighed) is sound and is kept as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: 'For 16-mark judgement questions, examiners reward weighing factors and reaching a defended overall view.'
findings.truth: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour. Rewritten as an instruction.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: '130 ships, around 24,000 sailors and soldiers' (repeated in the conclusion, a flashcard and a mark scheme). Also 'Eight weeks later the surviving fleet was being scattered by storms north of Scotland.'
findings.truth: The Armada carried about 10,100 sailors and 19,300 soldiers, roughly 30,000 men. And the fleet left Lisbon in late May, was north of Scotland in August and was scattered by the September gales, which is about three months, not eight weeks. Both corrected in all four places.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Spanish Armada' (10,138 sailors and 19,315 soldiers)

findings.claim: 'the Lord Chamberlain's Men and the Lord Admiral's Men were the leading troupes by 1588'.
findings.truth: Anachronism. The Lord Chamberlain's Men were not founded until about 1594, six years after the option ends. The leading company of the 1580s was the Queen's Men, formed in 1583, alongside the Lord Admiral's Men.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Lord Chamberlain's Men' (founded c.1594 under Henry Carey, Baron Hunsdon)

findings.claim: 4-mark mark scheme: 'the Lord Chamberlain's Men and the Lord Admiral's Men were the leading troupes'.
findings.truth: The same anachronism as F29, in indicative content a student would copy into an answer.
findings.evidence: as F29

findings.claim: 12-mark mark scheme: 'companies such as the Lord Chamberlain's Men and the Lord Admiral's Men needed an aristocratic patron'.
findings.truth: The same anachronism as F29.
findings.evidence: as F29

findings.claim: 'give two clearly distinct features — for example, the curriculum of grammar schools and their daily routine count as one feature, not two'.
findings.truth: Wrong advice that would cost marks. Curriculum and the length of the school day are two separate features, and this lesson's own mark scheme lists them as separate bullets. Changed to the real trap: two details about the same feature (two subjects on the timetable) count as one.
findings.evidence: lesson 9 practice_questions[0].marks

findings.claim: Mark scheme: acting companies 'needed patronage from figures like the Lord Chamberlain'.
findings.truth: Anachronistic for 1572-88, for the reason in F29. Changed to a nobleman such as the Earl of Leicester, whose company was licensed in 1574.
findings.evidence: as F29

findings.claim: 'both would harden into law only after Elizabeth's reign'.
findings.truth: The 1601 Poor Law was passed in Elizabeth's reign; the same lesson calls it 'the famous Elizabethan Poor Law'. Changed to 'at the end of Elizabeth's reign, in 1601'.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction in lesson 10 content_html

findings.claim: 'The Edexcel spec deliberately puts poverty alongside exploration and Virginia in Key topic 3 to make this judgement testable.'
findings.truth: An unevidenced claim about the board's intent. The factual half (Key topic 3 does contain all three) is true and is kept.
findings.evidence: spec, Option B4 Key topic 3

findings.claim: 'By the 1580s an English captain could plan a voyage to West Africa, the Caribbean or even round Cape Horn.'
findings.truth: Anachronism. Cape Horn was not rounded until 1616. Elizabethan ships used the Strait of Magellan, as Drake does two paragraphs later in this same lesson.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Cape Horn' (first rounded in 1616 by Schouten and Le Maire)

findings.claim: 'In April 1585 Raleigh dispatched Sir Richard Grenville with about 600 colonists and supply ships.'
findings.truth: About 600 men sailed on seven ships, but only about 100 were left on Roanoke as the settlement under Ralph Lane. Overstating the colony six-fold weakens the standard answer that it was too small and too badly chosen to feed itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Roanoke Colony' (seven ships, about 600 men sailed; about 100 stayed with Lane; Drake evacuated them, reaching England in July 1586)

findings.claim: 4-mark mark scheme: the settlement 'consisted largely of about 600 soldiers and gentlemen'.
findings.truth: The same six-fold overstatement as F37; about 100 men stayed.
findings.evidence: as F37

findings.claim: The 16-mark question says '(Spelling, punctuation and grammar will be assessed in your answer.)' and its mark scheme rewards SPaG in every band.
findings.truth: As F24: Paper 2 awards no SPaG marks. Removed from the question text and from all four band lines.
findings.evidence: spec: all 8 SPaG marks sit on Paper 1 Q5/6 and Paper 3 Q3(d)

findings.claim: 'On these "with SPaG" questions, accuracy and period vocabulary are rewarded'.
findings.truth: As F24: there are no 'with SPaG' questions on this paper. Rewritten so period vocabulary is still urged, without the mark claim.
findings.evidence: spec: all 8 SPaG marks sit on Paper 1 Q5/6 and Paper 3 Q3(d)

findings.claim: 'The Pearson 2026 terminology guidance asks us to write "enslaved person", not "slave".'
findings.truth: Invented provenance for a real house preference. The preference is kept; the fake citation is removed.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented provenance

findings.claim: 'a small Plymouth ship called the Pelican slipped out of Plymouth Sound carrying Francis Drake, a crew of 164'.
findings.truth: 164 was the whole expedition across five ships, as the lesson itself says four paragraphs later. Reworded so the Pelican leads five ships.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction in lesson 11 content_html

findings.claim: 'Each parish was to keep a register of births, marriages and deaths.'
findings.truth: Parish registers recorded baptisms, marriages and burials, not births and deaths, and the requirement dates from Cromwell's injunctions of 1538; 1559 restated it. Not worth an edit at GCSE, but the 4-mark mark scheme repeats it as a new 1559 duty.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Parish register' (England, from 1538)

findings.claim: 'archbishops of Canterbury and York at the top, then 27 bishops'.
findings.truth: The Church of England had 27 sees in all, two of them archbishoprics, so about 25 bishops. Left alone: 27 is the figure most textbooks quote for the dioceses.
findings.evidence: diocesan lists for the provinces of Canterbury and York, 1559

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Where and when was Sir Philip Sidney killed?' / 'At the Battle of Zutphen, September 1586.'
findings.truth: Sidney was wounded at Zutphen on 22 September 1586 and died of the wound on 17 October. The lesson body says 'the death of the poet Sir Philip Sidney', which is fair. Common textbook shorthand, so left.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Philip Sidney'

findings.claim: 'Bad harvests in 1586 and 1587 pushed already-fragile households over the edge' (repeated five times in the lesson).
findings.truth: 1586 is the well-attested harvest failure; 1587 is much less so, and the standard list of Elizabethan failures runs 1562, 1573, 1586 and 1594-97. Not corrected because sources vary and the ripple would touch six fields.
findings.evidence: standard harvest-quality series for Tudor England

findings.claim: Lesson 10 teaches the 1601 Poor Law and lesson 11 the 1587-90 'Lost Colony', both outside the option's 1558-88 span.
findings.truth: Both are clearly dated as later context, and the spec bullet examined is 'reasons for the failure of the first settlement in Virginia', which lesson 11 covers properly. Labelling rather than deletion is right, and the text already labels them.
findings.evidence: spec, Option B4 title and Key topic 3

summary: No lesson was clean. Every lesson set two practice questions in an 8-mark 'Explain why' form that Paper 2's British depth study does not use, and lessons 8 and 11 claimed SPaG marks on a paper that awards none. The substantive history errors cluster on Tudor descent (Mary, Queen of Scots called Henry VII's granddaughter twice), an invented count of Marian bishops, four fabricated examiners'-report citations, the Lord Chamberlain's Men placed six years before they existed, Alva sent to the Netherlands in answer to a war he preceded, and a Roanoke settlement overstated six-fold.
